lines.text: A reaction may appear rapid or slow, but we need a measurable meaning for that description.

Rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. Frequency of collisions is the number of collisions per unit time. An effective collision forms products, the particles collide with sufficient energy to overcome the activation energy and with suitable orientation. A non effective collision produces no reaction. Thus the rate follows the frequency of effective collisions, not simply the total number of encounters.
A product concentration that rises quickly has a greater positive gradient and a higher formation rate.
Rate equals change in concentration per unit time. Effective collisions produce reaction, non effective collisions do not. Frequency of effective collisions controls rate.
Why can many collisions occur while the reaction rate remains low?
Two experiments can contain the same chemicals yet proceed at different speeds when they are diluted or compressed.

Increasing the concentration of a reactant places more particles in each unit volume. The frequency of collisions rises, so effective collisions occur more frequently and the rate increases. For reacting gases, raising pressure by reducing volume at constant temperature also increases particles per unit volume, collision frequency and effective collision frequency. Lowering concentration or pressure has the opposite effect. At constant temperature the particles do not gain kinetic energy merely because concentration or pressure rises.
The key causal chain is particle density, then collision frequency, then frequency of effective collisions, then rate.
Higher concentration usually raises the rate. Higher gas pressure at constant temperature usually raises the rate. Both act through more frequent effective collisions.
Explain why compressing reacting gases at constant temperature can increase their rate without increasing their average speed.
A graph or table turns a visible change into a numerical rate that can be compared between experiments.

Use experimental data to calculate average rate as change in the measured quantity divided by elapsed time. For concentration data, the unit may be moles per cubic decimetre per second, for gas volume, it may be cubic centimetres per second. Convert minutes to seconds when needed. An instantaneous rate from a curved graph is the gradient of a tangent at the chosen time. A reactant concentration decreases, so use the magnitude of its negative gradient for a positive rate of disappearance. Use the balanced equation when converting a measured product rate to a different reactant rate.
For two H two O two aqueous yields two H two O liquid plus O two gas, peroxide disappears twice as fast in moles as oxygen appears.
Average rate equals change in quantity divided by elapsed time. Instantaneous rate equals tangent gradient at the chosen time. Convert units and apply the equation's mole ratio.

At constant temperature, compression increases the number of gas particles per volume, so collisions occur more often. A confuses pressure with temperature.

In one breath.

Rate tells us how rapidly reactants disappear or products appear. Changes in concentration or gas pressure alter how often particles collide effectively, while measurements over time let us calculate the rate.
Key ideas.

Rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. It can also be expressed as change in an experimentally measured quantity, such as gas volume, per unit time. Its unit depends on the quantity measured, a concentration rate may be moles per cubic decimetre per second, while a gas volume rate may be cubic centimetres per second. A positive rate of disappearance uses the negative of a reactant concentration graph's gradient because the concentration falls.

Frequency of collisions means the number of collisions per unit time. An effective collision leads to reaction and product formation, particles must collide with sufficient energy to overcome the activation energy and with a suitable orientation. A non effective collision produces no reaction. A large number of collisions therefore does not mean every pair reacts. The rate depends on the frequency of effective collisions.

Increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution puts more of its particles into a given volume. Reactant particles meet more frequently, so there are more effective collisions per second and the rate usually increases. Dilution reverses this effect. Increasing the pressure of reacting gases by reducing their volume at constant temperature also puts more particles into each unit volume. Collisions become more frequent and so does reaction. Constant temperature matters, increased pressure by compression does not itself give particles more kinetic energy. For a gaseous mixture, adding an inert gas at constant volume and temperature leaves the reacting gases concentrations unchanged, so it does not increase their mutual collision frequency.

The chord joins the curve at ten and sixty seconds, its gradient gives the average formation rate over that interval. The tangent touches the curve at twenty seconds, its gradient gives the instantaneous formation rate there. The curve becomes less steep as the reaction slows.
Method.
Identify the quantity measured and the start and end times. Subtract the starting value from the ending value. For disappearance of a reactant, take the magnitude of its decrease.

Divide the change by the elapsed time, average rate equals delta quantity over delta t. Convert minutes to seconds if the requested unit uses seconds. State the unit that follows from the measured quantity.

On a curved graph, an average rate is the gradient of a chord joining two times. For an instantaneous rate, draw a tangent at the specified time and calculate its gradient using two well separated points on that tangent.

When the measured substance differs from the substance named in the question, use the balanced equation. For two H two O two aqueous yields two H two O liquid plus O two gas, twice as many moles of peroxide disappear as moles of oxygen appear. At r. t. p. convert gas volume using V m equals twenty four point zero cubic decimetres per mole.
Worked example.

A product concentration rises from zero point zero three zero to zero point one five zero moles per cubic decimetre in forty seconds. Calculate its average formation rate. Change in concentration equals zero point one five zero minus zero point zero three zero equals zero point one two zero moles per cubic decimetre. Rate equals zero point one two zero over forty equals zero point zero zero three zero moles per cubic decimetre per second. This is an average over the whole interval, not the rate at a single instant.
Worked example, instantaneous disappearance rate.

A tangent at fifty point zero seconds on a reactant concentration time curve passes through open bracket ten point zero seconds, zero point three six zero moles per cubic decimetre close bracket and open bracket ninety point zero seconds, zero point one two zero moles per cubic decimetre close bracket. Calculate the instantaneous disappearance rate at fifty point zero seconds. Use these well separated points on the tangent, they need not lie on the curve itself. Gradient equals delta c over delta t equals open bracket zero point one two zero minus zero point three six zero close bracket over open bracket ninety point zero minus ten point zero close bracket equals minus zero point two four zero over eighty point zero equals minus zero point zero zero three zero zero moles per cubic decimetre per second. The negative gradient means the reactant concentration is falling. Its positive disappearance rate is minus delta c over delta t equals three point zero zero times ten to the minus three moles per cubic decimetre per second at the instant where the tangent was drawn, not an average over the curve from ten to ninety seconds.
Traps.
Trap, Every collision produces products. Why it's wrong, Some collisions lack enough energy or suitable orientation. Instead, Link the rate to the frequency of effective collisions.
Trap, More concentrated particles move faster. Why it's wrong, At constant temperature their energy distribution is unchanged. Instead, Explain the greater number of collisions per unit time.
Trap, Use the oxygen production rate as the peroxide disappearance rate. Why it's wrong, The balanced equation has a two to one mole ratio. Instead, Apply the coefficient before dividing by time.
Exam technique.

For Define, give a precise rate definition including per unit time. For Explain, connect the changed particle density to collision frequency, then to effective collisions and rate. For Calculate, show subtraction, time conversion, any mole ratio and the final unit. A product graph slopes upward, a reactant graph slopes downward, but report its disappearance rate as positive.
